label: fact-check
system: You fact-check the surprise claims planned for a short explainer video, before its narration is written. For each claim: verdict "keep" if the research notes support it as written; "reword" if the true version is close (give the claim with exactly the wording and numbers the sources support, e.g. "over 600 gallons" for a rounded figure, "New England" instead of a wrong state); "drop" if it is false, unsupported or a myth. Judge ONLY from the research notes (a claim they do not support is dropped) and copy the source URLs from them (url and title) for keep and reword.

Topic: escalator
Claims (index: claim | suggested search):
0: Escalators in the US are usually built at a 30 degree slope. | escalator standard incline 30 degrees ASME A17.1
1: An escalator's steps ride on two sets of wheels running in two tracks, which keep each step level. | escalator step wheels two tracks keep step level how it works

Research notes (from 3 web searches):
Claim 0: US escalators are usually built at a 30 degree slope. Supported in a corrected form: codes cap the incline at 30 degrees and 30 degrees is the standard angle.
- USC Illumin: the standard angle of inclination is set to 30 degrees. Source: https://illumin.usc.edu/elevating-experiences-the-role-of-escalators-in-public-spaces/
- Heavy-duty transit escalator spec: inclination not to exceed 30 degrees. Source: https://dcmpx.remotevs.com/net/railsystem/PL/heavy-duty-escalator

Claim 1: an escalator step rides on two sets of wheels in two tracks that keep it level. Supported as written.
- HowStuffWorks: each step has two sets of wheels on two separate tracks; the tracks are spaced so that each step will always remain level; a motor drives gears at the top that pull the chains. Source: https://science.howstuffworks.com/transport/engines-equipment/escalator.htm

Claim 2: safety codes require a brake that stops the escalator when power fails. Supported as written.
- Pennsylvania Code 7.324: each escalator drive shall be provided with an electrically-released, mechanically-applied brake which automatically stops the escalator if the circuit is opened. Source: https://regulations.justia.com/states/pennsylvania/title-34/part-i/chapter-7/subchapter-j/section-7-324
- California Title 8 section 3090: an electrically released brake shall automatically stop the escalator when any safety device functions. Source: https://dir.ca.gov/title8/3090.html
